Bootstrap Regression to predict glucose levels

Sebastian Ross

2026-09-12

1 Introduction

We analyse a dataset of 5,110 patients to study what factors are associated with average glucose level (avg_glucose_level, mg/dL).Elevated glucose is a well-established risk factor for stroke, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes; understanding which clinical and demographic variables co-move with glucose may help identify patients who would benefit from earlier screening and lifestyle intervention.

The data are from the Kaggle Stroke Prediction Dataset (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fedesoriano/stroke-prediction-dataset) and contain 12 variables: id: a unique identification number gender The gender of the person male, female or other age the age of the patient hypertension if the patient has hypertension heart_disease if the patient has heart disease ever_married if the person is has been married or not work_type The type of work that they do children, government job, never worked, private or self employed. Residence_type The type of residence a person lives in Rural or Urban avg_glucose_level The avrage glucose level of a patient bmi The BMI of a given patient smoking_status If a person smokes, never smoked, formaly smoked, or it is unknown. stroke If the person has ever had a stroke before

Our goal is to figure out which of our factors are associated with average glucose level and which are useful predictors.

url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Kingsoul42/STA-321/main/dataset/healthcare-dataset-stroke-data.csv"
stroke_predictions <- read.csv(url, header = TRUE)

2 Exploratory Data Analysis

ever_married, work_type, Residence_type,avg_glucose_level, bmi, smoking_status, and stroke are our character variables. We will be looking at the different variables looking for sparcety and know what we should do with those values. We will be looking at these different variables via bar graph to judge sparsity. We will also be looking at any of the variables to see if they make sense to be included in the model as predictor or not.

df <- stroke_predictions[, c("gender","hypertension","heart_disease",
                             "ever_married","work_type","Residence_type",
                             "smoking_status","stroke")]

ggplot(df, aes(x = gender)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 1. Gender distribution", x = "Gender", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(hypertension))) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 2. Hypertension distribution",
       x = "Hypertension (0 = No, 1 = Yes)", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(heart_disease))) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 3. Heart disease distribution",
       x = "Heart Disease (0 = No, 1 = Yes)", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = ever_married)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 4. Ever married distribution",
       x = "Ever Married", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = work_type)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 5. Work type distribution",
       x = "Work Type", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = Residence_type)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 6. Residence type distribution",
       x = "Residence Type", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = smoking_status)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Figure 7. Smoking status distribution",
       x = "Smoking Status", y = "Count")

Figures 1–7 show that most categorical variables are reasonably balanced. The only exceptions are gender == "Other" where there are only one observation. That is causing us to drop this observation due to that. We also see that work_type == "Never_worked"is vary sparse but we need to keep it given it would change the meaning behind work type. We also need to remove id as it is not a useful predictor given it is just a unique identifier not useful for prediction.

stroke_predictions$id  <- NULL
stroke_predictions$bmi <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(stroke_predictions$bmi))

stroke_predictions <- stroke_predictions[stroke_predictions$gender != "Other", ]

cat_vars <- c("gender", "ever_married", "work_type",
              "Residence_type", "smoking_status")
stroke_predictions[cat_vars] <- lapply(stroke_predictions[cat_vars], factor)

imp <- mice(stroke_predictions, m = 5, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
stroke_predictions_imp <- complete(imp, 1)
stroke_predictions_imp$hypertension <- factor(stroke_predictions_imp$hypertension)
stroke_predictions_imp$heart_disease <- factor(stroke_predictions_imp$heart_disease)
stroke_predictions_imp$stroke <- factor(stroke_predictions_imp$stroke)

3 Model Building

full_model <- lm(
  avg_glucose_level ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease +
                      bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type+ Residence_type + smoking_status,
  data = stroke_predictions_imp
)

backward_step <- step(full_model, direction = "backward", trace = FALSE)

null_model <- lm(avg_glucose_level ~ 1, data = stroke_predictions_imp)
forward_step <- step(null_model, scope = formula(full_model),
                     direction = "forward", trace = FALSE)
summary(forward_step)

4 4. Model Diagnostics

#model assumptions
par(mfrow = c(2,2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(full_model)

The residual plots show a non constant variance showing a distinct pattern and clustering. We also see the residuals are coming off the dashed line in the Q-Q plot. We also see that there are a couple of highly influental points that could be skewing the data.

5 Box–Cox Transformation

In this section we will be seeing if transformations might help solve so of our issues we see in the full model. For this we will do a box-cox transformation on our models. We will look at a graph and look to see what is a good value for the lamda we will use to transform the models.

boxcox(full_model, lambda = seq(-1.25, -0.5, by = 0.05))

From the graph we see that λ = −0.9 seems to be a good value for lamda with it being in the interval and is a convinent value to use.

\[ Y^{*} \;=\; \frac{Y^{-0.9} - 1}{-0.9}. \]

lambda <- -0.9
bc <- function(y) (y^lambda - 1) / lambda

stroke_predictions_imp$glucose_bc <- bc(stroke_predictions_imp$avg_glucose_level)

full_model_bc <- lm(
  glucose_bc ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease +
               bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type,
  data = stroke_predictions_imp
)

backward_bc <- step(full_model_bc, direction = "backward", trace = FALSE)
summary(backward_bc)

6 Model Diagnostics and Goodness-of-Fit

Here we will be looking for multicollinearity, if our residuals are normal as well as the goodness of fit for the model. We will be using vif function to look at the multicollinearity. We will be using Shapiro Wilks test and a Q-Q plot to look for normality of the residuals in our model. We will look at goodness of fit to select the best model for us to use. ## Multicollinearity (VIF)

From this we still see with the shapiro wilks test and the Q-Q plot that the residuals for this model are not normally distributed. ## 6.3 Goodness-of-Fit Comparison

select <- function(m) {
  e     <- residuals(m)
  n0    <- length(e)
  dfr   <- df.residual(m)
  sigma <- summary(m)$sigma
  SSE   <- dfr * sigma^2
  R.sq  <- summary(m)$r.squared
  R.adj <- summary(m)$adj.r.squared
  MSE   <- sigma^2
  Cp    <- (SSE / MSE) - (n0 - 2 * (n0 - dfr))
  AIC   <- n0*log(SSE) - n0*log(n0) + 2 * (n0 - dfr)
  SBC   <- n0*log(SSE) - n0*log(n0) + log(n0) * (n0 - dfr)
  X     <- model.matrix(m)
  H     <- X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)
  d     <- e / (1 - diag(H))
  PRESS <- sum(d^2)
  data.frame(SSE = SSE, R.sq = R.sq, R.adj = R.adj,
             Cp = Cp, AIC = AIC, SBC = SBC, PRESS = PRESS)
}
gof <- rbind(select(full_model), select(full_model_bc), select(backward_bc))
row.names(gof) <- c("Full (raw)", "Full (Box–Cox)", "Reduced (Box–Cox)")
kable(gof, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 1. Goodness-of-fit measures for candidate models")

7 Bootstrap Regression

Here we will be doing two non-parametric methods due to the issues we were saw in our model. We will be using Bootstrap by cases which resampleing method that looks at the individual cases of the original data set. The other would be Bootstrap residual this resamples based on the residuals in the model and pulling from there.

X <- model.matrix(~ age + hypertension + heart_disease +
                  bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type,
                  data = stroke_predictions_imp)
y <- stroke_predictions_imp$glucose_bc

fit_orig <- lm.fit(X, y)
beta_hat <- fit_orig$coefficients
names(beta_hat) <- colnames(X)
#bootstrap conventions
B      <- 1000
num.p  <- ncol(X)
samp.n <- nrow(X)

new_boot_mat <- function() {
  m <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = num.p)
  colnames(m) <- colnames(X)
  m
}

7.1 Case Bootstrap

btr_case <- new_boot_mat()

for (i in 1:B) {
  idx <- sample.int(samp.n, samp.n, replace = TRUE)   # resample rows
  fit <- tryCatch(
    lm.fit(X[idx, , drop = FALSE], y[idx]),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(fit) &&
      length(fit$coefficients) == num.p &&
      !any(is.na(fit$coefficients))) {
    btr_case[i, ] <- fit$coefficients
  }
}
btr_case <- btr_case[complete.cases(btr_case), , drop = FALSE]
cat("Case bootstrap:    ", nrow(btr_case), "/", B, "rows kept\n")
FALSE Case bootstrap:     1000 / 1000 rows kept

7.2 Residual Bootstrap

y_fitted <- as.vector(X %*% beta_hat)
resids   <- y - y_fitted

btr_res <- new_boot_mat()

for (i in 1:B) {
  y_star <- y_fitted + sample(resids, samp.n, replace = TRUE)
  fit <- tryCatch(lm.fit(X, y_star), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(fit) &&
      length(fit$coefficients) == num.p &&
      !any(is.na(fit$coefficients))) {
    btr_res[i, ] <- fit$coefficients
  }
}
btr_res <- btr_res[complete.cases(btr_res), , drop = FALSE]
cat("Residual bootstrap:", nrow(btr_res), "/", B, "rows kept\n")
FALSE Residual bootstrap: 1000 / 1000 rows kept

7.3 Histograms — Case vs Residual Side by Side

Each coefficient gets two panels: the case bootstrap on the left and the residual bootstrap on the right.

boot.hist <- function(bt.coef.mtrx, var.id, var.nm, scheme) {
  x <- bt.coef.mtrx[, var.id]
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]

  if (length(x) < 2 || diff(range(x)) == 0) {
    plot.new()
    title(main = paste0(var.nm, "\n(", scheme, ": no finite values)"))
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }

  x1 <- seq(min(x), max(x), length = 300)
  y1 <- dnorm(x1, mean(x), sd(x))
  hb <- max(hist(x, plot = FALSE)$density)

  hist(x, probability = TRUE,
       main = paste0(var.nm, "\n(", scheme, ")"),
       xlab = "",
       col = "azure1",
       ylim = c(0, max(y1, hb)),
       border = "lightseagreen")
  lines(x1, y1, col = "red3")
  lines(density(x, adjust = 2), col = "blue")
}

# 
par(mfrow = c(ceiling(num.p / 2), 4),
    mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1),
    oma = c(0, 0, 1, 0))

for (j in seq_len(num.p)) {
  boot.hist(btr_case, j, colnames(btr_case)[j], "case")
  boot.hist(btr_res,  j, colnames(btr_res)[j],  "residual")
}

We see here that both cases for the bootstrap methods show that the coefficients in the model are normal as you can see from the different graphs. With the our sample size being as large as it is the CLT is what causes these normal coefficients. We also see that the that the empirical and theoretical curves are relatively close showing that they are significant given the variables and p-values. ## Combined Bootstrap Summary

Here is where we will see a table that shows the differences between the bootstrap cases and bootstrap residuals and which of the non-parametric bootstraps is better for us to use. for these specific model.

ols_fit  <- lm(glucose_bc ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease +
                 bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type,
               data = stroke_predictions_imp)
ols_coef <- summary(ols_fit)$coef

## Align rows to the design-matrix column order
Estimate   <- ols_coef[, "Estimate"]
Std.Error  <- ols_coef[, "Std. Error"]
p.value    <- ols_coef[, "Pr(>|t|)"]
Estimate   <- Estimate[colnames(X)]
Std.Error  <- Std.Error[colnames(X)]
p.value    <- p.value[colnames(X)]

btc.ci.95 <- apply(btr_case, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
btr.ci.95 <- apply(btr_res,  2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
fmt_ci <- function(lo, hi) {

    sig <- ifelse(lo > 0 | hi < 0, "*", " ")
  paste0("(", formatC(lo, format = "g", digits = 3),
         ", ", formatC(hi, format = "g", digits = 3), ")", sig)
}
coef_tbl <- data.frame(
  Estimate   = Estimate,
  Std.Error  = Std.Error,
  `Pr(>|t|)` = p.value,
  btc.ci.95  = fmt_ci(btc.ci.95[1, ], btc.ci.95[2, ]),
  btr.ci.95  = fmt_ci(btr.ci.95[1, ], btr.ci.95[2, ]),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names   = colnames(X)
)

kable(coef_tbl,
      digits  = c(5, 5, 5, NA, NA),
      align   = c("l", "r", "r", "c", "c"),
      caption = "Table 3. Regression coefficient matrix with OLS inference and 95% bootstrap percentile intervals")

8 Discussion

Here we are going to see what we need to look and see what the scale of the model because of the transformation to see the true scale of the average glucose.

back <- function(y_star) (lambda * y_star + 1)^(1 / lambda)

mean_glu <- mean(stroke_predictions_imp$avg_glucose_level)
y_star_0 <- bc(mean_glu)

b_htn <- coef(backward_bc)["hypertension"]
delta <- back(y_star_0 + b_htn) - mean_glu
b_age <- coef(backward_bc)["age"]
deltaa <- back(y_star_0 + b_age) - mean_glu
b_heart <- coef(backward_bc)["heart_disease"]
delta_heart <- back(y_star_0 + b_heart) - mean_glu
b_bmi <- coef(backward_bc)["bmi"]
delta_bmi <- back(y_star_0 + b_bmi) - mean_glu
b_gender <- coef(backward_bc)["gender"]
delta_gender <- back(y_star_0 + b_gender) - mean_glu
b_ever_married <- coef(backward_bc)["ever_married"]
delta_ever_married <- back(y_star_0 + b_ever_married)
b_work_type <- coef(backward_bc)["work_type"]
delta_work_type <- back(y_star_0 + b_work_type)

cat(sprintf("At mean glucose = %.1f mg/dL, hypertension is associated with a %.4f mg/dL change.\n",
            mean_glu, delta))

            mean_glu, deltaa))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, age is associated with a 0.2737 mg/dL change.

            mean_glu, delta_heart))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, heart disease is associated with a NA mg/dL change.
cat(sprintf("At mean glucose = %.1f mg/dL, bmi is associated with a %.4f mg/dL change.\n",
            mean_glu, delta_bmi))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, bmi is associated with a 0.5081 mg/dL change.
cat(sprintf("At mean glucose = %.1f mg/dL, gender is associated with a %.4f mg/dL change.\n",
            mean_glu, delta_gender))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, gender is associated with a NA mg/dL change.
cat(sprintf("At mean glucose = %.1f mg/dL, marrige status is associated with a %.4f mg/dL change.\n",
            mean_glu, delta_ever_married))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, marrige status is associated with a NA mg/dL change.
cat(sprintf("At mean glucose = %.1f mg/dL, work type is associated with a %.4f mg/dL change.\n",
            mean_glu, delta_work_type))
FALSE At mean glucose = 106.1 mg/dL, work type is associated with a NA mg/dL change.

We see that from this how hypertension increases the average glucose levels based on what we see above how it is affected by each factor. When we see NA those are our character variables that are not put at a different scale by the transformation.

Some caveats for this is one we needed to remove the gender == "Other" with it being the only observation with that value causing some issues. Another was we removed stroke as a predictor variable with it being post-treatment. We also see from the bootstraps that both are reasonable but due to the non-normality of the residuals make the case bootstrap over the residuals. We also see that in the final model that never worked was insignificant it is necessary for understanding the other work types. This is different form ever married this is likely a predictor that if we were to make another model we would likely want to remove it

9 Summary

We looked at 5109 observations after the removal of our one gender == "Other" observation. For this model we used the MICE package to impute the missing bmi values for those given patients. From there we used a Box-Cox transformation with λ = −0.9 to the average glucose levels and ran both a forward and backwards step wise where both ended up with the same predictor variables. With the diagnostics we ran on the residuals we see heteroscedasticity which shows we should be using the bootstrap case method over the bootstrap residual methods. The bootstrap case having a wider confidence intervals for the most part also show that we should be using it over residuals. The bootstrap case and bootstrap residuals being close choices shows the robustness of our conclusion.

10 Practical Recommendations

Given the strong associations with age, hypertension, heart disease, and BMI with glucose show that living a healthier life style with losing weight and lowering blood pressure seem to have a large influence on glucose levels. We would also want to collect more information on people with the gender == "Other" to make see if other is an influence with it being essentially a fitted value. We also would want find more people who had never worked to see if we can fix the sparsity issue and make them more useful in inferences. We would want to make sure that we these results are verifiable by other groups. We should also look to see if possible to not impute values try and see if we could collect those and get more information.
